the core of one of the major reasons advanced by the hon. member for passing this bill. It is not my desire to repeat the arguments which have been advanced, but certainly when a member like the hon. member for York West, with the position he holds, makes a statement in this chamber which in the opinion of other hon. members is fallacious, the other members should have the privilege of probing into the extent of his knowledge. That is the reason I asked the question. I will just say this. No doubt he has got off balance. He just has no information on this matter.
He wants to put the price of gold on the speculative market. I will just use one illustration and then I will say no more unless he provokes me. All you have to do in order to know what happens to the price of a commodity when it is on the open market is just remember what used to happen to the wheat crop in western Canada when the price of wheat was on the free exchange in Winnipeg. Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask a question or two. I was interested in listening to the exposition of the point of view of the hon. member for York West. I heartily disagree with his statement that it would benefit the Canadian people to have a return to the gold standard. I support what the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre said.
I want to draw to the minister's attention the suggestion that came from another direction and was unique, and I want to get his opinion on it. The hon. member for Comox-Alberni, when speaking on this subject in the house on February 12, 1951, made a most interesting and original contribution to the debate.
Somebody has to have some intelligence around here.

He suggested that if gold were staked out in ore bodies, the government could issue a certain amount of currency against the gold in the ground. That was not a frivolous remark, Mr. Chairman. I am sure it was made as the result of a good deal of thought and meditation on his part.

It would be the first time.

The suggestion came from a distinguished member who sits on the front bench, a gentleman with considerable business experience, one with a good parliamentary record and who is an original and creative thinker. I want to ask the minister this question. Has the minister given consideration to the proposal made by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni? If so, what objection would he have to an economic system or monetary and fiscal policy such as that suggested by the hon. member for Comox-Albemi?

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I do not see that this question is directed to, or deals in any way with, the question that is before the committee.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Are you speaking for your party?

I am afraid the hon. member for Kootenay West has not read his Hansard. I am sure he can read; and I am quite sure that his powers of analysis are such that if he read a quotation from my speech at that time he would realize that what I said was this. Wo were setting up a manpower council at that time in order to try to allocate manpow er to most essential uses in Canada. I said that if we were short of manpower for the defence of our country, I thought probably the first thing we could divert was the manpower from gold mines in Canada. I still believe that to be so. Happily, however, since that time we found that we had sufficient manpower to maintain our gold mining as well as our other projects as far as national defence is concerned.
The hon. member will also recall that I did not say that paper should be issued against gold lying in the ground. I said that if it was necessary for Canada to have gold backing its paper dollars-and that is something for which I am quite prepared to take the word of the economists on the government benches-if we were short of manpower, I thought possibly we could take proven gold ore reserves in the ground and use those at their net value for the issue of paper currency. I still believe that to be possible.

I should like to ask the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys several questions. The first is this. What proportion of the gold production has been going into the so-called free market for non-monetary gold since the policy was inaugurated last fall?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: The production figures for the last quarter of 1951 and the first quarter of 1952 for auriferous mines were 1,126,738 ounces and 1,071,930 respectively. The percentage sold in the free market-
I would prefer it if the minister called it the premium market, because it is not truly free.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: The percentage of total production going into the free market in the last quarter of 1951 was 25-7; in the first quarter of 1952 it was 32-5.

What does the government estimate to be the effect on the production of Canadian gold of the inauguration of the so-called free market for non-monetary gold last fall; the effect on the total production?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext:
A possible increase or
decrease? I would not like to express an opinion on that. I do not suppose it makes any difference. Some mines are taking advantage of the free market. Eleven mines during the last quarter of 1951 and I think twelve at the present time have elected to use the free market.

That was my next point, Mr. Chairman. Why should that be? Why not allow the mine free choice each quarter as to whether it will market its gold production on a monetary basis or on a nonmonetary basis?

Is that the settled decision of the government in this matter, that they are not going to open this up at all to allow a free election each quarter?

Then I take it that it is not the intention of the government to alter the

present plan, or to permit an entirely free election each quarter on the part of each
mine?

my question. I understand what the minister is saying about the present basis. If a mine does elect to go on the non-monetary marketing basis it is bound for the balance of the calendar year, no matter in what quarter of the year it so elects?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys

I am amazed to hear the minister say that, because obviously he has not been reading the statements made by very eminent figures in this field. Why does the government insist that gold marketed on the so-called nonmonetary basis should be debased to a fineness of 22 carats or less, in finding its way to this so-called free market?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys

To what customers is the minister referring in making a statement like that? The essence of this matter is that the Canadian gold producer, in order that his gold may go to this so-called free market for non-monetary gold, must debase it to a fineness of 22 carats or less. It simply means that he has to add copper to it. Then when it is sent out of the country to the purchaser it is refined. What sense is there in that? Why should not the Canadian gold producer be permitted to sell gold on this free market on the same basis as he sells it for monetary purposes? Why introduce this requirement of debasing, knowing that when it reaches the foreign purchaser it is simply going to be refined again?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
When the committee adjourned on Friday last I was dealing with some of the points that had been under discussion during the consideration of these estimates. I believe I can cover the remaining points in a very few minutes. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre again raised the question of pensions for retired employees of the Canadian National Railways, and frankly I must say to him that I cannot see the point in his argument nearly as well as I could a year ago. The position I have taken all along is that this is- a matter for the officers of the Canadian National Railways to determine with its employees.
I say that I cannot see the point of the hon. member bringing it up again this year, because the position is entirely different now than it was then. For instance, the hon. member said he must draw the attention of the government to it until something is done. Something has been done; something very tangible has been done. The pension rules of the Canadian National have been revised very substantially and very favourably, I understand, to the men. They have been revised in two ways: First, by amendments to part I. Part I provides a basic pension and the opportunity of contributing to a supplementary pension. Employees may also transfer from part I to part II. Second, by part II of the plan which was designed to give employees the opportunity of increasing their pensions.
I think I could do no better than to put on the record a statement made by Mr. Donald Gordon, the president of the Canadian National Railways on Tuesday, April 29, 55704-156
Supply-Transport
in the committee on railways and shipping, which appears at page 111 of the report. He said:
Now, these men you are talking about did not choose to take advantage of that opportunity and that is why when their services terminated they received this small basic pension.
He is referring to the $25 per month basic pension.
That pension is now augmented to an extent by the old age pension and that brings the amount received up to as much as $65 a month. And now, as regards the C.N.R. increasing the basic pension, that would be meaningless, it would simply mean that the C.N.R. would be paying the additional sum instead of the provinces paying it. Most of these people would become eligible at age 65 or over. In connection with that I may say that the labour representatives supported our view on this point and in that respect I would like to quote to you from a letter.
Then he is asked about the date of the letter, and he says the letter is dated March 31. I should say that this letter is from Mr. Hutchinson, who is chairman of the brotherhood committees. The letter reads:
The expressions of opinion appeared to be almost universally in approval of the improvements which have been made.
Some of those who did not contribute toward annuities expressed disappointment that their lot is not improved but could not seem to impress the meeting that they were entitled to very much consideration on account of the fact that they had not made any effort to improve their lot.
Then Mr. Gordon goes on as follows:
Now that, as I say, is the view of the men themselves in a meeting assembled on this specific point. And so far as the C.N.R. management are concerned, we do not feel that we have any obligation in logic to recommend an increase in these so-called basic pensions by reason of the changed position arising out of the old age pension plan; because, again I emphasize that with a means test involved, if we were to increase the pension then it simply means that the C.N.R. would be paying the increase and not the provinces.
So much for the attitude of the management of Canadian National Railways.
Then the hon. member says this question must be considered by the minister and by the cabinet for action by the government without delay. Well, the cabinet and the minister considered this very thing. The management of the Canadian National Railways submitted a revision of their pension plan. We saw no objection to it, in fact we approved it after giving it careful study and said, "Go ahead; we think it is an improvement." The hon. member says it is for me to act. I do not think it is. The Canadian National Railways management means something or it does not. It has been appointed to administer the system and the affairs of its employees, and surely there must be a division of things. There may come a time when further changes are suggested. When changes are suggested, as I have said in the

Supply-Transport
house and as I repeat now, it will then be the duty of the government to consider the requests or recommendations made by the officers of the Canadian National Railways. If the men, in conjunction or in co-operation with the management, want to submit to the government an additional plan to increase or revise the basic pension, the government will give it consideration. The government will not necessarily turn it down. The position I have taken all along is that it is for the management to determine what action should be taken. They have determined the action that should be taken, they have referred it to us, and we have approved of the position. For the time being I think the matter should be considered in that light.

speechtext: Does the minister feel that this question is sub judice?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: Unquestionably it is.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If it is sub judice, he cannot refer to it. I do not remember the incident. I think it might have taken place while I was absent from the chair. I do not recall the point of order having been raised.

On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, may I say that one matter the hon. member for Bow River raised was the fact that the trucking association was not given a hearing or might not be given a hearing before that board, and whether or not an amendment to the Transport Act should be brought down' at this session in order that the board of transport commissioners might hear the trucking association. I would point out that, according to a Canadian Press dispatch this morning, the truckers have been refused a hearing. It has already been decided, by a ruling of the board of transport commissioners, that the trucking association cannot be heard

before that board. Because that ruling has been made, I would say that particular aspect is certainly not sub judice now.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
I am not going to deal with that point because the board is still sitting and will sit tomorrow on the case. I happen to know that. In any event, that was one point only that was decided before the case proceeded to the evidence stage. But since those people made representations to me personally I think I could deal indirectly with them without perhaps touching on the points that are now before the court. It will not, however, be a complete answer to my hon. friend.
The point arises out of an agreement made between the railways and certain oil companies in the province of Saskatchewan for the transportation of their oil and petroleum products. The requests of the truckers, to me at least, were that they should be allowed to appear before the board. The statement of the hon. member for Bow River was to this effect. Why should not the truckers be allowed to appear when the railways are allowed to appear before municipal boards in the various provinces? Of course, the answer to that is quite clear. The act indicates who is a carrier, and it was the act passed by this parliament. The provincial municipal board also defines those who may appear, and in the case of the Canadian National Railways it so happens that they own trucking operations in some of the provinces and are therefore free to appear. The definition is quite clear, I think.
Then it was suggested that the government should amend the Transport Act in order to allow them to appear. The government gave careful consideration to that suggestion after the representations made to them by the Canadian Automotive Transport Association, with a particular representation from the province of Saskatchewan. Here I pause to say that no one made stronger representations on behalf of them than did the Minister of Agriculture and the hon. member for Regina, in support of the contention that these truckers should be allowed to come in and make their case. The government carefully considered the point and came to the conclusion that it would soon have to determine the broader question of whether or not, following the recommendations of the royal commission on transportation, it should take over interprovincial and international trucking or in other words regulate those forms of trucking. Since a decision on the one question would have meant a decision on the broader question, we thought that, at this time at least, we should not decide in favour of allowing them to come in as a carrier. If we had done so, I think there was a neat constitutional
55704-156J
Supply-Transport
point in that we might well have been told that we were infringing on provincial rights since, by the definition of carrier, we were attempting to regulate to some extent provincial operations of truckers.
Then again the act, to which I do not want to refer in detail, clearly covers the point raised by my hon. friend, namely that anybody who, being a carrier or a shipper, feels that he is aggrieved or affected, can protest before the board of transport commissioners; and I understand that is what is being done now. There are a number of shippers who are not parties to the agreement with the Canadian National Railways or the Canadian Pacific Railway and who are at the moment protesting against it. I cannot go any further because, as I say-
May I just ask a question of the minister?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: May I just finish my statement. As I say, I cannot go any further because the case, as my hon. friend knows or should know, is before the court.

The question I wanted to ask the minister was this. While some of these companies are appearing before the board, it is only through the courtesy of the board that they can do so, it is not? They have no legal right to do so.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I have covered that point. My hon. friend was not in his seat when I did so. Perhaps he will look at my remarks as they appear in Hansard.
I did not know the minister was going to be on tonight or I would have been here earlier. I was in my room, and I came down as soon as I knew he was on.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: The other point raised by the hon. member for Peace River is one that I feel I should deal with because I think he has and I say this with great deference- and for the lack of a better word let me say magnified the dangers to the province of Alberta in so far as the present position with regard to transcontinental rates is concerned. The position as I understand it is this. The one and one-third rule has not been disturbed in the slightest degree by any decision of the board. The one and one-third rule still remains. What has been done is that a very small number of transcontinental rates have been increased by the two railways.
Can the minister say how many?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: Well, I would think roughly eight or ten, but I am guessing when I sav that.

The key commodities, though.

Supply-Transport

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
On commodities such as iron pipe, canned goods and fish. My hon. friend says "key commodities". The categories of key commodities have been changed. For instance, while carloads could be moved on a transcontinental rate from one part of the country to the other, in certain instances it is not possible to move a carload of 60,000 pounds but one may move 30,000 pounds or 40,000 pounds. This I think does not entirely eliminate the benefit of the rates that existed before. The point I want to deal with is this. The benefit of the one and one-third rule still remains. I think what my hon. friend was aiming at was the fact that the board heard and determined the application made by the three or four western provinces with reference to the $7 million subsidy. It heard that, and there was a difference of opinion between Manitoba, which argued in favour of a per 100 pound basis subsidy, and the other provinces, which argued in favour of a percentagewise subsidy. They maintained that since freight rates had increased by percentages, they should also decrease in so far as the subsidy was concerned by percentages. The board found a formula which took into account the 100 pounds idea and the percentage idea. It was a compromise which seemed to be agreeable, as I understand it, to all the provinces save Alberta.
I am informed that Alberta launched an appeal against that decision. Since then I am told the province of Alberta has withdrawn its appeal, which would indicate to me that the advantages to be gained by the decision of the board under the $7 million subsidy are satisfactory to the province of Alberta.
There is one other point I wanted to make, namely that the board is still continuing the investigation under P.C. 1487. It is hoped that under that it will be possible to equalize freight rates, and undoubtedly out of the equalization the province of Alberta, as other western provinces, stands to benefit a great deal.
The hon. member for St. John's West raised one or two problems with reference to the Port aux Basques ferry. That work is proceeding satisfactorily. There was a change in the design which caused some delay, but since then that has been ironed out, and I am informed by our officers that the plans for construction are going ahead quickly.
With reference to the two coastal steamers of the Bar Haven type, the Canadian National Railways, who are charged1 with the responsibility of operating those steamers, have asked for tenders. Those tenders are being considered now and the contract has not been awarded1.

There are a number of other detailed questions which the committee would not expect me to deal with at this moment. I think I can dispose of them at a later date.
May I ask the minister about the questions asked by the hon. member for Cumberland?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Yes; the hon. member for Cumberland dealt with a number of questions, one of which was in regard to the closing of certain stations. All I can say there is that stations are closed by order of the board of transport commissioners. Hearings are held before the board, and no doubt the particular station to which my hon. friend has reference was dealt with in that way. I presume that before the station could be closed the railway in question, the Canadian National Railways or the Canadian Pacific Railway, would have to make application to the board; and it is the board, not the department, that determines the question.
He also dealt with the dieselization of locomotives and the protection of the coal mining industry of Nova Scotia. Well, that is a broad question, with which the president of the Canadian National Railways dealt at length in the committee on railways and shipping.
I would refer my hon. friend to the sessional committee of railways and shipping, and particularly the hearing on Tuesday, April 29.
He also asked that I make a statement with reference to power resources and development in the province of Nova Scotia, as raised by the hon. member for Westmorland. I would not attempt to deal with that. The Department of Transport is not charged with the responsibility for power development. True, it is interested in questions of that nature, but it would not be a matter for me to handle in this department.
With reference to the contribution of the province of Nova Scotia to the causeway project, about which the hon. member inquired, it is $5,500,000.

If I may clear up these questions, he also asked about the possibility of double tracking the Canadian National line from Moncton to Truro and through to Sydi-ney, referring particularly to the line from Truro to Sydney. In addition, he asked for a statement about the position of the Chig-necto canal and about the Amherst airport, and then about shipbuilding in Nova Scotia.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: Well, it is pretty difficult to cover all of that.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: We will give you another forty minutes.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
With reference to the double tracking, that is a question which comes up

fairly regularly in my estimates. Again, it was dealt with by the president of the Canadian National Railways, I think fairly effectively, at the sittings of the committee. All I can say now is that the fact it has come up in the house requires me to bring it again to the attention of the officers of the railway, which I shall do.
With reference to the Chignecto canal, there is no change. A reference was made to the royal commission on transportation, and I need not repeat what the royal commission found in so far as that project is concerned. They made a recommendation. The committee is familiar with the report. Everyone has the report, and the recommendation can be found there.
With reference to the Amherst airport, if I remember rightly that airport is being turned over to the Crown Assets Disposal Corporation.
It is a municipal airport.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: My recollection is that the airport in question has been requested by the municipality. In other words they want the return of the land so that they can use it for municipal purposes. As I remember the correspondence with the hon. member for Cumberland and the mayor of Amherst is to that effect. I may be wrong. My recollection of the whole matter is that the land in question is to be assigned to the Crown Assets Disposal Corporation so they may return it, sell it or dispose of it to the municipality.
Perhaps the minister can check that. I take it from the purport of the hon. member's question that what he was asking for was help for the airport, an improvement of the airport.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: I will check on it.

I should like to say a word or two in connection with the statement the minister has made. I thank the minister for the information he has given in connection with the freight rates situation, but I think perhaps he was in error when he suggested that Alberta had withdrawn the appeal against the board's division of the subsidy because we appeared to be satisfied with that division. Actually the reason the Alberta government withdrew its objection was that the Canada Steamship Company appealed the case against the board. That case is proceeding now, I understand, and therefore I cannot discuss it. As a matter of fact we in Alberta feel that when the board made its decision in respect to the division of the $7 million subsidy, partly on the basis of percentage and partly on the per 100 pounds involved basis, they were yielding to the interests within the city of Winnipeg and
Supply-Transport
were considering their welfare in preference to that of the whole of western Canada, particularly in Saskatchewan and Alberta. That matter was argued fully before the committee; and I am quite sure the people of Alberta feel that was an unfair division of the $7 million.
There was another point I wished to mention to the minister, and it is this: The whole burden of the main part of my statement the other day was that, without any change in the competitive situation in the past six or seven months, the Canadian Pacific Railway did file with the board a new schedule of transcontinental rates on seven or eight key items and that the Canadian National Railways, which all through the committee hearing last fall took the position the railroads could get by without increasing the transcontinental rates and could apply the one and one-third rule without it affecting their revenue, changed their position.
It was not very long, in fact the ink was not dry on the legislation we passed, until the Canadian Pacific had somehow or another inveigled the Canadian National into supporting it in posting a new schedule of rates. As I said the other day, the Canadian Pacific could not have done so alone; they had to have the support of the Canadian National. Here is our own Canadian National system rushing in before they had even given the new one and one-third rule time to be tried, to find out what the experience would be. They proposed, with the Canadian Pacific, a new schedule of rates which we think is completely unjustified.
As the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra said, this affected a considerable number of important items, such as canned goods. Whereas the merchants in Alberta under the one and one-third rule in the transcontinental rates in effect until early this year could receive their canned goods from Toronto or other Ontario areas for $2.09, it has now jumped to $2.53.
Some of us predicted that in committee.
But British Columbia is paying the most.

The fact that it came about was not, I suggest, as a result of the prophetic powers of the hon. member so much as because of the weakness of the Canadian National Railways in permitting themselves to be led around by the nose by the Canadian Pacific. That is the protest I was making the other day. I say they went in, with indecent haste.

You would not expect them to have different rates, would you?

Supply-Transport

No, I would not expect them to have different rates, because the Canadian Pacific simply would not dare operate under a different schedule of transcontinental rates from the C.N.R. That is why I say the culpable people are the Canadian National people; they could have held the line by simply saying, "Look here, you Canadian Pacific people, we took the position we could get along; and we would like to wait until we see what the experience is going to be. In any event it will not be serious for the time being. When we discover what the experience is, and how it will affect our revenue, we will be in a position to say whether or not we will join you in posting a new schedule of rates."
That is all that was necessary. Certainly the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific cannot, under the circumstances, try to operate on different schedules. That is why they got together. As I said the other day, before such an important step was taken, even with a small group of items such as the eight or ten mentioned, in view of what happened last fall and the position taken by the minister I think the Canadian National people should have gone to him and sought his advice before agreeing to join the C.P.R. in posting new rates.
You could get those canal boats running again.
We ought to get something going. I do not know what the outcome of the Canada Steamship Lines case will be; but when that has been decided Alberta will make her decision with respect to her position.
No, to C. D. Howe.

I am quite prepared to give the minister credit for almost anything, but not for the weather. I am prepared also to pay a tribute to the government and the minister for the encouragement they have given to the use of that particular route. Some hon. members appear to be intensely political in connection with almost any matter raised in this house.
There are one or two things which still militate against the use of this route and which I think could be remedied. I believe there are about four altogether. If this port is to be successful there must be import as well as export trade. Import facilities would seem to be limited during the time export operations are being carried on. Nevertheless I believe there are import facilities at the port which are not being used to their full extent. I would urge business firms, chambers of commerce and boards of trade throughout the prairies to encourage the use of this port. It is their own port and they should make greater use of it.
The Saskatchewan government has done something in the way of setting an example. In connection with bringing in heavy machinery or other imports from England they have ordered them brought in through that port. This created some savings to themselves and to the taxpayers of the country. If private
Supply-Transport
business firms would follow that example greater use would be made of the port. Of course they are doing that to a limited extent.
Then there is the matter of the necessary annual importation of stevedores, dockers and other labour to take care of the loading of the wheat and the unloading of imports. The solution of this problem is the further development of the whole north. I think Canada's future lies in the north. When the north country is developed in whatever way it can be developed there will be more population. There would be a greater population at Churchill and we would have a native supply of labour to handle loading grain in what is an all too short navigation season.
At present these men must be brought in from Montreal; and while I am ready to admit that they do the work satisfactorily I have heard of one or two instances where they have seemed to regret having to work at a little place like Churchill. They have indicated that they thought it was rather small potatoes. I think we would do better if there was a labour force living right there and taking some pride and interest in the port.
Then another thing is the lack of feeder lines to the port. If one looks at the map he will see there are certain gaps. We would like to see a network of east and west lines leading into The Pas in Manitoba, which is the railway centre through which the grain is shipped. In his remarks the other night the hon. member for Melfort referred to two lines, one from Reserve Junction to Arbor-field and the other from Melfort to Carrot River. We look forward to the time when those lines can be extended to The Pas.
Another thing which is hindering the use of this port by grain companies and individuals is the diversion charges on grain passing through Churchill. My own definition of these charges is that they are money paid for services not rendered. The savings made by using Churchill, and they are very considerable, are cancelled out by these diversion charges. I do not know what the amount is, but I believe it is about a cent and a half per bushel. I want to say in the strongest words possible that these charges are unnecessary and iniquitous. They should be abolished. In connection with this hindrance to the use of this route I should like to quote from the Alberta wheat pool budget which under the heading of "Churchill Savings" states:
On wheat exported through the port of Churchill on Hudson bay during the 1950-1951 crop year the wheat board received an average premium of 4-96

Supply-Transport
cents a bushel on wheat sold under the International wheat agreement and 3 05 cents a bushel on class 2 wheat, over the Fort William-Port Arthur price. The board1 made a saving of $132,217.22 on freight on grain exported through this port but paid $139,560.91 in diversion premiums. This information was given in the House of Commons by Right Hon. C. D. Howe.
My hon. friend referred to him a moment ago. When I raised the matter with the Minister of Trade and Commerce 'he did not agree with me that these charges were iniquitous. There is one other short quotation on the same subject which I should like to give. It is from our local paper, the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix. In an editorial on April 5 it expresses the view held by most western people with respect to this matter. The editorial reads as follows:
The existence of a diversion charge is bad enough in normal times. It means that the western farmer is making a donation to the terminal elevators at the lakehead and receiving nothing in return. It is one of the numerous obstacles that have been placed in the path of the development of Churchill, thereby preventing to some extent the growth of trade through the port with its consequent saving to prairie wheat growers. In short the farmer is paying to have himself kicked. But in this year when every facility of the trade has been necessary to move the crop it is a national scandal to pay money for service which the lake-head terminal could not provide in any case.
I say this impediment to the use of the port of Churchill should and must be removed. As I said before, I am grateful for such support of the route as has been given by the Department of Transport and the wheat board, and I urge that this support be continued and increased. Not only do I say this on behalf of my own city and my own province but also on behalf of all Canada, because a doubling of the present use of the facilities at Churchill with respect to the shipment of export grain would relieve the Canadian public of the present deficit which it has to pay. It is true the deficit has been decreasing, but it is still a considerable amount.
I only wish to take a very few moments. As usual my comments are nonpolitical.
At this time?

I see the parliamentary assistant to the minister laughing. I think he should know better because as a good friend of mine and also a very capable parliamentary assistant he will not mind my having made that reference. I do not think there will be any controversy about what I have to say. I wish to deal with two particular items. Like other backbenchers in the house I welcome the opportunity provided by the estimates to discuss a matter which I think is of interest to every hon. member. I want to refer first to transportation by private airline companies.

Only today I received a letter from the minister in answer to one of mine. I might remind him that when I am attending the house he need not send my letters to Camlaohie. The word is hard enough to pronounce, let alone spell, but when I am here he might address letters to me at the House of Commons. I know he will not take exception to that remark.
The matter I wish to raise concerns more than the particular case I have in mind. Recently a lad from Sarnia booked passage on the Queen Charlotte Airlines from Vancouver to some place a little farther north, though I thought Vancouver was far enough north for any white man to live. I see no exception is taken to that statement. The plane crashed and the young lad was killed. The minister was good enough to send me the general order of the air transport board covering the situation. The lad was a passenger on a private airline, and the same situation might arise with anybody's son or daughter or even with ourselves.
In looking at what material was available to me, I was rather disturbed to find that people taking transportation by such companies were limited in the amount of any claim they might make, and probably more so than, any of us may have thought was the case. I know the minister will correct me if I am wrong, but it does not seem fair to me that a private airline company operating anywhere in the Dominion of Canada should be so privileged as they seem to be under these regulations. The liability of the air transport company is limited to a passenger liability of $20,000 per seat. I have had occasion at different times to travel on some of these private transport planes when I was in a hurry to get some place, and there were more passengers than there were seats. I think that in itself is important, though I do not say they should not be overloaded because at times we all want to get some place and we do not worry about it. I do not think that such a limitation on liability is fair to the people who travel by private airlines. I more or less felt that in taking transportation by such means people were fully covered. If I am wrong I know the minister will correct me, but I do not think the limit is high enough.
I have no explanatory notes covering this particular matter, but I cannot see why there should be such a limit in the case of any transportation company. Certainly most people carry some insurance, and I have always felt that when people travelled by air in this country or elsewhere the transportation company was liable for damages to the

degree that might be held fair in a court of law, and that the family of the person involved would be entitled to receive damages to that extent in any court in the land. I know the minister will investigate this case further, but I should like to point out that under general order No. 3-51 so far as public liability is concerned the limit for one person is $20,000 with a total of $40,000 per aircraft. I am going to say quite frankly, Mr. Chairman, that I do not think that is fair. I do not think it is a businesslike proposition to place before the Canadian people. I am inclined to the idea that this sort of legislation may have originated when air transportation or even sea transportation were in their infancy, but I should like to see a complete revision of the legislation. I do not think it is fair to the Canadian people or to anyone else who might be travelling on a Canadian line.
The other item to which I wish to refer, Mr. Chairman, concerns property damage. Under this same general order No. 3-51, there is a limitation of $5,000 per aircraft per accident. I shall moderate my language in describing that limitation, and say that I believe it is extremely unfair, that is if I am interpreting the order correctly. All too often in recent months we have found property damage running much higher than that when accidents have occurred. I am not going to pursue that argument because I think it is so apparent to everyone in the house that this order should be overhauled in order to permit a guarantee that would be in keeping with Canada's status. It would be regrettable if an accident occurred in which some people suffered damages as high as $25,000 or $50,000, and this limitation enabled the company to set its liability at such a small amount. I am not going to pursue the matter, Mr. Chairman, but I think it is one of those things to which we should give some study today. While it may not have been drawn to the attention of the department before, it seems obvious that this order needs revision.
The other point to which I shall refer, Mr. Chairman, is something that I think applies to all of us. I rather hesitate to mention any particular incident-I am not going to refer to the item when it is called-but I should like to refer to the subject of damages that might accrue to any person or persons as the result of a fire or other accident to a passenger boat. Not so many years ago there was such an unfortunate occurrence, apparently through no fault of the captain, who was a most capable officer. Perhaps I should refer to the particular incident so hon. members will know to what I am referring. I
Supply-Transport
refer to the fire which occurred on the steamship Noronic while it was docked in Toronto. Court actions were instituted both in Canada and the United States. Most of the passengers were United States citizens. In this country we welcome the United States citizens as tourists, whether they come by car or any other mode of travel.
The point I am making is this. I believe the liability of a steamship company for damages is limited according to the tonnage of the boat. In this particular instance the ship was carrying several hundred passengers and a certain amount of freight. While any court in the Dominion of Canada may have found damages, and rightly so, to the extent of several millions of dollars, we find that under our present legislation the steamship company's liability was limited on some tonnage basis. It has occurred to me that perhaps the limitation was proper years ago when we had sailing vessels, but it seems to me that in this advanced stage of our development we must recognize our responsibility. I believe the government has a responsibility to see that any passengers who desire to take a vacation on a Canadian ship are not faced with such a limitation on liability as this legislation seems to impose.
There is no limitation in the case of gross negligence, is there?

It is a long time since I studied any law, so I am not going to enter into an argument as to whether or not there was gross negligence. That would be a matter for the courts to determine. The point I am making is this. I am not going to argue the point about negligence, but wherever a disaster occurs the people should not be faced with such restrictions with regard to liability as are now apparent. I think that is unfair to any passenger who may embark on a cruise, no matter whether it be in Canadian or international waters. I may be wrong in my assumptions but after all, Mr. Chairman, I know from my personal knowledge that because of the limited liability in the particular disaster to which I referred some families who were left with two or three dependents received only $2,000 or $3,000 as damages, whereas in our own courts, for whom we have the greatest respect and where there is no limitation for damages in actions other than those of this sort which are limited by order in council or by a statute, they could have received a great deal more.
If I have misappraised this idea I am sorry, but I am now only going on what I know has happened. I feel that we in Canada should take it upon ourselves through the government to see that regulations and
2480

Supply-Transport
restrictions with respect to damages arising from accidents, either on airlines or on the sea, be revised at an early date.

Mr. Chairman, may I take a few moments to speak on a subject which was mentioned by the minister when he spoke in the chamber on Friday last. I refer to the question of a water connection between the town of Yarmouth, Nova Scotia, and a port in the New England States. I do not intend for a moment to review, as I have on previous occasions, all the various factors affecting this situation; but I think the committee should realize that when I raise this matter I am discussing a service that has been in effect between Yarmouth and the New England states for over fifty years.
When world war II came along the service was discontinued because of the need for ships for overseas purposes. Following world war II the service was re-established1 on a part-time basis. The service operated only in the summer months, whereas prior to 1940 it had run both summer and winter. Following the war the ships had only been in service for a year or so when the owners, the Eastern Steamship Lines, announced that they intended to sell their ships at the first opportunity.
When you have had a water service for some fifty years or more you can imagine what it does to business in that area when it is learned that the service may be discontinued. AH avenues were explored and on December 7, 1949, the Minister of Transport announced that an automobile-carrying ferry would be built to operate between Yarmouth and a port in the New England states. Of course that announcement was a great relief to Nova Scotians in general and particularly to those of us who live in the southwestern end of the province.
Then in June, 1950, the Korean outbreak took place. Some two or three months later it was necessary for the minister to announce that, because of the steel shortage, it would be necessary to postpone the building of the ferry. Then, in the early spring of this year the papers ini the province of Nova Scotia and in the New England states were filled with articles to the effect that the sale of the Eastern ships had been practically consummated, that the ships would not run this year, and there would be no service between Yarmouth and Boston.
Prior to that time, during that period and since then the provincial government, municipal councils, boards of trade, town councils and various service organizations have all passed resolutions urging that the new

ferry be built as soon as possible so we may be assured of a continuity of service. It is easy to imagine how upsetting it is to business-retail business, wholesale business, hotels, motels and to everyone who is in any type of business-when it is realized that a ship may or may not run; that you may or may not have tourist traffic from the United States to Nova Scotia; that you may or may not be able to travel from the United States to Nova Scotia by water; that you may or may not be able to ship your goods by water, because you do not know-and we do not know-from one month's end to another what the situation is going to be.
It was not until May 8 of this year that Eastern Steamship Lines announced that they were running their ships again this year, but there is no guarantee for next year. The length of service is cut down this summer to two and a half months, and no one knows what is going to happen in the summer of 1953. As I said before, this situation is very upsetting to business.
No thinking person questions for a moment the fact that there is a shortage of steel. Despite articles and editorials ini many of the papers by those who purport to have some information on the subject, I think there is general agreement that there is a shortage of certain types of steel, particularly of steel plate, in structural shapes. I think that is the term the engineers use.
The minister has announced that there is nothing in the estimates this year for the ferry. This is most upsetting to Nova Scotia. We realize that there is a steel shortage, particularly of structural steel plate.
I should like to make this suggestion. The minister has already mentioned the fact that plans and specifications are completed and that we-"we" being the government- will be able to get under way quickly once the steel shortage eases or is over. May I say that it has been my experience-rather short though it may have been in this field- that after an announcement is made, it takes many months before advertisements are placed, tenders are called and the contract is awarded. I should therefore like to suggest to the minister, on behalf of Nova Scotians in general and those of us who live in western Nova Scotia in particular, that notwithstanding his previous statement, he discuss this matter with his colleagues and give serious consideration to calling for tenders at an early date.
I believe it cannot be gainsaid that the amount of steel plate required between now and the end of the present calendar year, that is if one were to start to build the ferry within the next two or three months, would

not be very great, in fact it would be negligible. If I am not mistaken the statement was made in this chamber, by a colleague of the Minister of Transport, that by the end of this calendar year there will be an easing of the steel situation, that steel production in Canada will have increased by about 25 per cent and that early in 1953 the short or tight steel situation should be over.
All I ask of the minister is that he seriously think of reconsidering his statement of last Friday, that he do not give me an answer tonight, but that he rise in his place within the next few weeks and say: "I think that was an excellent idea, and we will call for tenders."

I first of all should like to agree with the suggestion made by the hon. member for Saskatoon. I believe that more use could and should be made of the port of Churchill. It has certainly meant a saving in the shipment of wheat, apart from the diversion charges.	The people in my part of the
province, with regard to the shipment of wheat, do not benefit to any extent from the port of Churchill but I believe the people in western Canada feel that the port of Churchill is their port, no matter to what extent they may use it, and the people in the three prairie provinces would like to see the port of Churchill used to the greatest possible extent.
The government is deepening the St. Lawrence waterway system. The country is spending a good deal of money on that project. Unless positive encouragement is given to the use of the port of Churchill I am afraid the St. Lawrence seaway development may spell doom for that port. For the life of me I do not know why the diversion charges are maintained. It does help the elevator companies but certainly it keeps the port of Churchill at a disadvantage, as compared with other ports, with regard to the shipment of grain. As the hon. member for Saskatoon has said, I believe every possible thing should be done to see that in the navigation season the port is used to the fullest possible extent.
I should like to deal for a moment with the statement of the minister that an amendment was not being made to the Transport Act in order to give the trucking association the right to appear before that board. I do not intend to refer to anything that is sub judice. I do not intend to refer in any way to the agreed charges which that board is now considering, or to say whether they are too low, too high or anything else. All I want to press for at the moment is an amendment to the Transport Act whereby the trucking association as of right may appear before that board when an agreed charge 55704-157*
Supply-Transport
is being discussed which affects the trucking industry. I do not think any association, or any group of people, should be condemned to economic loss without a hearing. Because of the way the act reads many truckers are condemned to economic loss without a hearing. Many of them are condemned to economic ruin, because they are small operators owning only one or two trucks, and at present they are not able to appear before that board and present their case.
The minister said that if an amendment were brought in to allow the trucking association to appear before the board of transport commissioners, then the government would have to give consideration to bringing the whole trucking industry under the Transport Act. Well, I do not think the giving of consideration to one amendment needs to be postponed or delayed because the minister or the government perhaps would like to bring in the broader amendment. If at any time in future the parliament of Canada feels that the trucking industry from one end of Canada to the other should be brought under the Transport Act, then that proposition can be dealt with at that time; but I hope that the government will now give further consideration to amending the Transport Act so the trucking association may have the right to appear before the board of transport commissioners whenever an agreed charge is being discussed that affects them very disastrously.
When I was home at Eastertime I discussed this matter not only with truckers, but more particularly with the consumers in Saskatchewan, the farmers of that province. While the farmers in our province may gain from any agreed charge, whether it is a matter of oil rates or some other agreed charge, nevertheless I believe I am correct when I say that these consumers are very much concerned that the truckers, their neighbours in the little towns who depend upon trucking oil and gas and other commodities, may at this time, or at any other time, be forced out of business because of an agreed charge. And they said to me without exception they felt that the truckers should have the right to state their case, and they added the further hope that any agreed charge that is entered into should be of a long-term nature and should not be raised after the competitor is put out of business. That is all I rose to say, Mr. Chairman. I want to impress upon the minister again the need for an amendment to the Transport Act so that at this time the trucking association will not be condemned to economic loss without a hearing.

I will take only a moment or two of the time of the

Supply-Transport
committee tonight to bring to the attention of the minister two or three items that we in western Ontario are particularly interested in. Last winter, just prior to the beginning of this session, representations were made to the board of transport commissioners regarding a dangerous crossing one mile north of Hyde Park, where the Canadian National Railways cross No. 2 highway. The representatives of the board of transport commissioners, the Canadian National Railways and the Ontario department of highways, together with the deputy reeve of the township of London and myself met there, and it was generally agreed that, all other systems of accident prevention having failed, steps would be taken to instal a warning light system. I have looked through the estimates and cannot locate any funds for that purpose, but I am hoping it will not be too late to include them in the supplementary estimates, if they are not in these estimates.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: May I tell my hon. friend that they would not be in these estimates, in any event; if it has been approved by the board, the Canadian National Railways or the body ordered by the board to do it would do it.

Thank you. The other item dealing with crossings has to do with a dangerous subway west of Melbourne known as the devil's tunnel. The Ontario department of highways have been improving highway No. 2 both east and west of this particular subway, but nothing has been done there, no doubt because of the fact that some changes are or will be contemplated at that particular spot. It involves a bit of an S turn, and the subway is too narrow for two cars or a truck and car to pass. I am hoping that will be taken care of in the not too distant future.
Then there is the question of the Canadian National Railways shop at London, Ontario. Railways seem to be a bit of a law unto themselves, apparently. The provisions of the Ontario factory act do not apply to that shop, apparently. I have received complaints of some of the conditions there. Provision should be made so that the Ontario factory act will be applicable, and an inspector sent in so that industry, which is no different from any other steel or heavy industry, would be subject to the same provisions and regulations as any other industry. No doubt the minister will look into this, and an improvement will be made.
I should now like to deal with a subject that was brought up earlier; and here I join the hon. member for London who brought the matter to the attention of the minister in the first place. I have refrained from saying anything about it because I was hoping that

the proposed weather station at London, Ontario would also be taken care of. I understand from items in the newspapers that such is not the case. Many groups all over western Ontario feel the need of an improved weather service at London. I am going to mention agriculture first. The western Ontario district has more and more gone into the growing of cash crops. All these cash crops are dependent on weather in the spring and fall, in the spring for planting and in the fall for harvesting. They are very dependent on knowledge of when frosts are likely to occur. The city council, the county councils and the aviation officials all have pointed out to the department, I believe, the need of such a station there. I have a long brief here from the fruit and vegetable growers of Ontario. I am not going to take time to read it to the committee at this point. However, it does set out in detail the needs of the industry in that area. I am hoping that further consideration will be given to the matter because the people in western Ontario are vitally interested in it.
Then, returning again to the railways and the Canadian National shops, there is the question of vacations with pay. This of course revolves around the length of service a man has given to the company. But there is a certain amount of dissatisfaction in the matter. I mention it to the minister so that he may look into it.

Mr. Chairman, under this
general administration item of the Department of Transport I am afforded the opportunity of placing on record a few questions which, at a later time, the minister may choose to answer. They concern the Canadian Pacific railway crossing in North Rose-dale section of Toronto.
Within the last twelve months in Toronto at least 500 of my constituents filed a petition with the mayor and board of control complaining about noise, vibration and other alleged nuisances attendant upon railway operations connected with the crossing at MacLennan Hill in the area known as North Rosedale in my constituency. This petition was passed through me from the mayor of Toronto along to the board of transport commissioners, with the result that an investigation was launched immediately.
The exact details of the investigation have not been revealed fully. If at a later date the minister chooses to do so, I would ask him to tell the committee something about that investigation by the board and its officers, as well as the findings made. It has been said, to the credit of the board, that a shortterm remedial solution has been found for the complaints of my constituents. Among other

things reference has been made to a fifteen mile an hour slow order placed against trains operating at the crossing. Those are trains of the Canadian Pacific Railway. I believe, too, that some prohibition has been laid down concerning whistling.
However I would ask the minister to confirm on the records of this committee just what has been ordered by way of a shortterm solution, and to give any other remedies the board has seen fit to order in the matter by way of a solution.
Then, too, my constituents are most interested in a long-term solution of the problem. It has been stated that the Canadian Pacific Railway plans discontinuing its present yards feeding the railway line in question, and to remove the yards from Lambton to some other location. I have been unable to get more information on this point. If at a later date the minister could see his way clear to report to this committee, I know it would be appreciated by my constituents. At the moment the leader of the petitioning group states that the matter is settled on a short-term basis to the satisfaction of those who associated themselves with him in bringing the matter before the board of transport commissioners. However, the long-term solution of the problem, that is the removal of the yards from Lambton to some other place, is a matter which I shall leave for the attention of the minister.

Mr. Chairman, on Friday last when the estimates of the Department of Transport were first before us, due to the interest I have in transportation matters it was my intention to make some extended remarks. However, after listening to so many speeches, I noticed that the minister was not paying too much attention. I took my cue from that and, after making a sort of gentlemen's agreement with him, decided that I would wait and ask my questions when the several items were called. I interviewed the chairman at that time and understood from him that I would have an opportunity. It was pointed out to me that, so long as my questions were relevant, I would receive answers.
Therefore I shall not take my forty minutes on this occasion-and in this I know I shall please the minister very much indeed.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: Thank you.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to bring to the attention of the minister, through this committee, a matter that has been raised in committee before both by myself and my predecessors. At the last session of this parliament I placed a question on the order paper, and repeated it at the beginning of this session, with reference to the union
Supply-Transport
station at Brockville. I received an answer finally on March 19 confirming what I had already known. The answer showed that this matter is indeed worthy of consideration both by the railways and the board of transport commissioners.
According to the answer I received, the station was built in 1860. Well, as a matter of fact it was built a few years before that. In fact, if it were not such a homely, decrepit, worn-down, dirty, old brick building, I believe I would call the attention of the Minister of Resources and Development to the fact that it might be designated as a national monument. But one does not designate relics of that type as monuments.
Beginning in 1875 the union station at Brockville was used by the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Grand Trunk Railway, the latter of which, as we know, is now absorbed in the Canadian National Railways system. I consider the station not only a disgrace to the Canadian National but also a menace to the town of Brockville. The facilities for mail, baggage and express are inadequate and obsolete, and make for very difficult working conditions for those who have to operate these railway services. Brockville is now a junction point for pool trains running between Toronto and Ottawa and Toronto and Montreal. At Brockville Canadian Pacific passengers leaving Ottawa on the day train to go to Toronto have to change to the Canadian National, while passengers on Canadian National trains in the afternoon and evening, from Toronto to Ottawa, have to change at Brockville to the C.P.R. The facilities for passengers who have to change cars constitute a hazard to the travelling public.
I consider both the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National lucky in that they have not had to pay heavy damages for personal injuries. I saw one man slip under a C.N.R. train coming into the station; and had it not been for a trainman standing right beside him there is no doubt both his legs would have been cut off. That is not good enough for the middle of the twentieth century; that is not good enough for a railroad system which is competing with bus and air transport. If the railroads insist on giving service like that they are bound to lose more and more of their passenger traffic.
From the standpoint of those living in Brockville the worst aspect is that when trains enter the station, especially east-bound passenger trains, the main artery of traffic leading from the south end of Brockville to the north is blocked. I want to pay special tribute to the train crews for their valiant efforts to do everything humanly possible to either split the trains or get them

Supply-Transport
moving as fast as they can. But the fact remains that road traffic is blocked, sometimes over the legal limit, which I believe is eight minutes when a main artery of traffic is concerned.
Brockville is a progressive, fast-growing community. Because of our location on the bank of the St. Lawrence river our growth must be to the north. The new housing developments are north of the main line of the Canadian National. Should a serious fire break out in this new area-and we have had two serious fires in Brockville within the last two years-I hate to think what the consequences might be if the fire department could not get across the tracks. I realize that they would split the train, but it might take a few minutes and it does not take long for a fire to spread. Then if there was a case of emergency illness and an ambulance was held up, either on the way to pick up the sick person or on the way back with the sick person to the hospital, a delay of a few minutes might mean the difference between life and death. Another particularly bad feature is that our children have to go to the other side of the tracks to get to school, and they are continually passing back and forth.
One method of relieving the situation would be to build a subway. In 1945 the municipal council applied to the board of transport commissioners and a plan for such a subway was devised. Brockville is built on preCambrian granite and as a result the cost of such a subway would have been in the neighbourhood of $1 million, the town's share being $300,000.
Another solution would be to move the station further east so that trains would not block this main artery of traffic. If that were done, not by the wildest stretch of the imagination could that old derelict which the Canadian National chooses to call a station be moved. It would mean a new station, which expense would have to be borne entirely by the Canadian National Railways because the Canadian Pacific use the facilities of the station on a lease basis.
Some other method might be devised, such as an overhead bridge; or another location might be picked. In fact another location has been picked, but it would be a little out of the way. However, it would be much cheaper than what was suggested by the engineers of the board of transport commissioners and the Canadian National Railways.
I understand there is a possibility that the province would help in the construction of a subway or overhead pass where the road .concerned is an integral part of a provincial
[Mr. Fulford.i
highway. Perth street, Brockville, is definitely an integral part of highway No. 29. The fact remains that no matter how this is done, the time has now been reached when this hazard must be eliminated. I am not prepared to say how it can be done. As I say, the town did apply through the usual channels in 1945 to the board of transport commissioners, but the cost was found to be prohibitive.
After all, the municipalities of Ontario are hit hard enough as it is. Our tax rate at the moment is 86 mills, and to undertake anything like this would increase the mill rate. The town is not in position to undertake any such financial deal. I implore the minister to explore every possible channel in an effort to devise means of eliminating hazards such as this. I have no doubt that similar hazards exist elsewhere in Canada, but I think I can guarantee that there is no worse menace to be found anywhere in the dominion than exists in the county which I have the honour to represent in this house.
Anyone who has taken the pool train during the day from Ottawa to Toronto or from Toronto to Ottawa will agree with what I have said about the conditions prevailing at the Brockville station. I think they will admit that I have not exaggerated in any way. Anyone who has travelled on highway No. 29 and has had occasion to use Perth street, Brockville, I think will admit that I have understated the hazard that exists.
There is one other matter which I should like to bring to the minister's attention, a matter which I have mentioned before. I refer to the necessity of having a weather station somewhere in the upper St. Lawrence valley. Totally different weather conditions prevail in the St. Lawrence valley from those in the Ottawa valley. At the present time the Brockville radio station broadcasts the weather reports issued for Haliburton, simply adding twelve hours to the report. I do not know what method is used by the local newspaper, but I can assure you that it is equally unsatisfactory.
When the St. Lawrence seaway is completed it will be vitally necessary to have a weather station in the upper reaches of the St. Lawrence valley. Inasmuch as this station will have to be built eventually I urge that it be built as soon as possible so that our farmers may have the benefit of accurate weather forecasts.

I should like to bring one or two matters to the attention of the minister, matters which I have discussed before. One is in connection with the Canadian Pacific Air Lines plane which was blown up in

Quebec. The widow of the pilot of that plane who lost his life lives in my constituency, and she has asked me to find out from the minister just what is the responsibility of Canadian Pacific Air Lines Limited. She lost her husband. I wonder if any of the other passengers or crew members on that ill-fated plane have received compensation. She applied for some expenses and was turned down. I believe she was promised employment with the Canadian Pacific, but she thinks she is entitled to something for the loss of her husband. At the present time the only compensation she receives for herself and her boy is from the compensation board of the province of Quebec. When the minister is answering questions I should like him to go into the details.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: I cannot hear the hon. member.

I am sorry. When the minister begins to answer questions I would appreciate it very much if he would go into that matter a little bit and tell me what it is possible for this lady to do. She is a widow with a son to raise, and I should like to know if any of the other passengers or crew members have received compensation. It is an unusual incident. The plane was blown up. It was the plane with which Guay was involved.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: I am familiar with the case.

I will detain the committee for only about three minutes for the purpose of asking the minister if he can exert some influence in a certain direction. We recognize that the minister has tremendous responsibilities. His department is large, and as it has to do with transportation by rail, air and boat, with all the ramifications that are involved, his work is great and his responsibilities are heavy. I rise at this time to point out one little need in a certain part of the country. I refer to the Canadian Pacific railway station at Calgary, Alberta. I am well aware that the minister has no particular jurisdiction over a private railway company, but I am also well aware that as Canada's Minister of Transport a word from him in the right direction will do wonders.
I am not raising this question because I desire to embarrass the Canadian Pacific Railway. I happen to be an old C.P.R. man. I had a happy relationship with the company when I was one of the ticket clerks in the Calgary C.P.R. depot thirty-five years ago. I renew acquaintances every time I go through that depot; but, Mr. Chairman, it is the same kind of depot now that it was thirty-five years ago. Hardly a stick of wood in the whole place has been replaced. Perhaps the
Supply-Transport
bars have been taken down from the ticket windows, and I think there are one or two new telephone booths. It is not only a matter of the building itself. The accommodation available for passengers is the worst of any station from Montreal to Vancouver, and I have visited them all.
There is no underground passage to enable you to reach a train on track 2, 3 or 4 if there happens to be a train parked on track 1. Let me give an illustration that may sound astounding to the minister. I arrived in Calgary one night on my way to Edmonton. The train was a little late because it was wintertime and nearly all the trains were late. I came in on the northbound train from Lethbridge and arrived at Calgary at about 10.30. The berths were made up on the midnight train to Edmonton. Do you know that I had to remain in the depot for nearly two hours before I could get on the Edmonton train and go to sleep. There was no underground passage, and as one train went out another train came in. For some reason the officials did not split any of the trains in the middle so that one could walk over the tracks. Therefore we had to wait there for two hours before we could go to bed because we had to cross to track 3 or 4 and there was a train on track 1 or 2.
Somebody may say that I should have complained to the railroad officials. I could have done that but if I had, perhaps I would have got some worker into trouble. However, my heart was brimming over with compassion, and instead of getting anyone into trouble I stayed in the depot and suffered for a couple of hours. I have actually seen people climb up the steps of railway cars, pass through the entranceway and step down on the other side in order to reach their trains. I have seen trainmen boost rather stout ladies up the steps so they might get over to track 2 or 3 in order to get their train on the other side. I do not know what the regulations are, but if an accident should happen when that was being done I am afraid there would be an awful mess not only on the platform, but someone would get into trouble and there would be a mess in that respect.
I know I am sometimes given to a little levity in the house, but I am serious when I say that a city the size of Calgary, which has doubled its population in the past ten or fifteen years, still has the same passenger accommodation as far as depots are concerned as it had thirty-five years ago.
We have the same as we had ninety-two years ago.

Then I will back my hon. friend in getting a new station if he will back me in getting a new station at Calgary.

Supply-Transport
Perhaps there will be a double amount of influence there. I am serious about this matter. It may be there are some things that I do not know anything about. Perhaps they are negotiating for a union station. If they are, for goodness sake let the negotiations be speeded up and some conclusion reached. So far as the C.P.R. is concerned, Calgary is on the main line. Every transcontinental train on the Canadian Pacific Railway passes through Calgary in addition to numerous local trains running north, east, south and west. That is the situation which exists. Therefore I say to the Minister of Transport that I wish he would look into the matter and use all the influence he can to get a new railway depot that will be adequate to supply the needs of a city the size of Calgary, Alberta, the oil capital of Canada.
Hurrah!
Hurrah!

Mr. Chairman, when the minister's estimates were first being considered I asked him some questions concerning Canada's merchant navy. He was good enough to give a brief reply that same evening, but I should like to get one or two points concerning that statement cleared up. On page 2321 of Hansard for May 16, 1952 the minister is reported as having said that there are now forty-five 10,000 ton ocean-going cargo vessels and twelve 7,500 ton vessels sailing under the Canadian flag. This would make a total of 57 ships. Is that the correct figure at the present time, and are all of those ships the old, slow vessels which were built during the war?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: The answer to that is yes, plus other ships such as the "Lady" boats of the Canadian National Steamships, diesel passengers and some tankers, making a total of 80. They are all the Park vessels of wartime construction.
And there are 97 Canadian-owned ships of the same type which are operating under the British flag, I understand. Is that the correct figure?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: That is correct.

The other evening the minister mentioned that two large modern tankers are under construction here or for which contracts have been let. Could he tell the committee what company is building those tankers, where they are being built, and on which coast they are to operate?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: They are for deep-sea operation on the Atlantic coast. They are being built by Davie Shipbuilding for the order of the Andros Company.
Into what service are they going, out of what port?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: For the Atlantic and Mediterranean service.
They will not be operating out of east coast ports.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: Yes, they will be operating out of east coast ports. They will operate out of Atlantic ports and in the St. Lawrence, depending upon where the cargo is going.

In my remarks the other night I brought up the replacement plan which was proposed by the Canadian maritime commission some years ago. The main purpose of that plan, as I read it in the second report of the commission-and I am referring particularly to page 52-was that Canadian owners, having sold these old, slow wartime ships, would pay the money into a trust fund held by the government or some government agency and with that fund it would be possible to build modern, fast cargo vessels to compete with the modern vessels of other maritime nations.
For example, on page 52 of the report we find these two statements:
The object of the plan Is to reduce and modernize the Canadian flag fleet.
Then again:
The funds, however, must be used for the purpose of replacement or modernization of Canadian shipping, and for the acquisition of vessels which are economic to operate.
