Incidentally, the minister himself is on record in different speeches two or three years ago to the effect that Canada must have a modern cargo fleet. I have here a quotation from a speech he made at the Canadian National Exhibition in Toronto in October, 1949, in which he said:
It has been the policy of the government to endeavour to maintain a merchant marine under a Canadian flag, owned and operated by Canadians. It is not the intention to support a large fleet, nor is it a question of national pride of ownership. It is considered that a small, efficient, modern fleet of ocean-going vessels would be of benefit to Canada, not only as a contribution to the national economy but for the purpose of national security.
That statement is in line with the recommendation of the Canadian maritime commission. However, the policy seems to have changed, particularly with regard1 to the replacement fund. Of course there is the fact that no single modern cargo vessel has been built for the Canadian merchant navy, either from that fund or any other fund in Canada to date.
I have here the fourth report of the Canadian maritime commission; the one that was tabled in the house last year. There we find that the replacement fund is now being used

for other types of shipbuilding. There appears to have been some provision made for assigning these funds, for example, to operators on the great lakes rather than insisting that they be used for the building of modern ocean-going cargo vessels. We find on page 6 of the report that the commission's policy is to allow only a proportion of the cost to be met by assignment of the funds held in escrow under its replacement plan where the assignment of funds is destined for the building, conversion or acquisition of other than ocean-going ships.
What I should like to know is what steps have been taken at the present time by the Canadian maritime commission or by the government, either under this replacement plan or under any other plan, to help bring about the construction of modern fast cargo vessels for the Canadian merchant navy. The minister will answer that question later, will he?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: Yes.	.

I raised also the question of the Canadian maritime commission. I was protesting that a chairman had not been appointed, except for the deputy minister of transport. I should like to repeat that I have a great respect for the deputy minister, and I think he is doing a grand job. But it was never our understanding that an important commission such as the Canadian maritime commission should have as its head the deputy minister or any other officer of the department. There is no parallel situation. For example, the board of transport commissioners is an independent body. There is no suggestion that the department should have any representative on the board. While the air transport does not have the independent status of the board of transport commissioners in that it is directly responsible to the government, nevertheless that air transport board has a separate chairman whose only job, as I understand it, is to act as chairman of that board.
We believe that the Canadian maritime commission should be in the same position. We believe there should be a chairman who has no other work to perform than that of supervising the business of that commission. Since the discussion the other evening I have been reading the annual report from the deputy to the minister, and at page 7 I find this statement:
By order in council P.C. 6063 of December 13, 1950, the undersigned was appointed a member of the Canadian maritime commission and made chairman thereof, thereby knitting more closely together the advisory and operational responsibilities of government with respect to marine transportation.
Supply-Transport
That statement would make it appear that it is the policy of the department to operate the Canadian maritime commission with the deputy minister or some other officer of the department as the chairman. I should like to know whether that is to be the fixed policy of the government. If it is, I am afraid it is an unsound one. I think shipping is of sufficient importance to this country for us to have a full-time chairman of the Canadian maritime commission. If it is of sufficient importance to have a commission at all, then there should be a full-time chairman.
I would point out to the minister that in the report of the Turgeon commission on transportation we had a finding with regard to these three important bodies, namely the board of transport commissioners, the air transport board and the Canadian maritime commission. The Turgeon commission explained the importance of each of those bodies to Canada, and went on to recommend that there should be only one body to deal with transportation, including the railways, the shipping and the airways.
I do not agree with that recommendation with respect to shipping. Coming as I do from a seaport, I consider that the shipping problems of Canada are of sufficient importance for us to have a separate commission. We are greatly worried because of the fact that, instead of having an independent commission to carry on the good work that was started, we now have one which is absolutely operating under an officer of the Department of Transport. The result is that the commission is, in effect, only a branch of the department. I would ask the minister to explain whether that is to be a permanent policy or whether we can expect to have some person appointed as the full-time chairman of this commission.
I repeat the recommendation I made the other night, namely that the minister try to get one of the leading shipping men of Canada, a leading marine lawyer, or someone whose life has been devoted to shipping. If that is done I think great benefit would accrue to shipping and to the country at large. I repeat that I am not for a minute questioning the ability of the deputy minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: Did the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra say that he had another question?

I have one other question on shipping. Then I have a question on an entirely different matter. This other question has to do with the notorious Ming Sung ships. As the chairman knows, they were, and perhaps still are, owned by a Canadian

Supply-Transport
company known as the Ming Sung Industrial Company which is controlled by Chinese citizens in communist China. I should like to know whether those ships are still on Canadian registry or whether there has been any change in that registration. Can the minister answer that question?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: I think my hon. friend should proceed in the usual way.
All right.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: I think he should ask his questions; then when he is through, I will deal with them.

All right. If they are still on Canadian registry, then as I read the Canada Shipping Act they are not only entitled to fly the Canadian flag but are bound to do so; if they do not, they break the Canadian law. I would refer the minister to section 89 of the Canada Shipping Act. If I am correct in that statement, it seems to me that something should be done about it by the Canadian government. If these ships are Canadian vessels then, as I say, they are entitled to fly the Canadian flag and are entitled to the protection of the Canadian navy, if you please-and I presume to the protection of the British navy and possibly of the allied navies. Yet the latest word we had of them was that they were in Canton, which is a communist-held port, waiting for a chance to make a break up to Shanghai, another communist-held port.
I realize that the situation is difficult, but I believe some steps should be taken to clear it up. I believe there is power to do so under the Canada Shipping Act. If not, there is certainly, under the Emergency Powers Act, power to deal with that unfortunate situation. I would ask the minister if he would explain the present status of those ships.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: Does that cover the questions my hon. friend wishes to ask?
That covers the shipping questions.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: Are those all the questions my hon. friend has to ask?

The other question has to do with the great lakes. I was surprised to read in the press of May 16-and I am reading now from a report in the Globe and Mail- an article which is headed: "Damage $1 Billion; Truman Calls on Army to help Lower Lakes." That dispatch was from Washington. The first paragraph reads as follows:
President Truman called on army engineers today to provide a remedy for high water damage to property on the shores of the five great lakes.

The article also gave particulars of the damage that was being done, and ended up with this paragraph:
Canada has agreed to the rediverslon of one of the two rivers flowing into Superior. It announced within the last few days that the Ogoki river would be diverted, on a temporary basis, to the Hudson bay watershed.
Today I picked up the current issue of U. S. News and World Report. It is dated tomorrow, as a matter of fact, May 23. I find an article in it entitled "Great lakes: new flood threat. Damage already big. Billion loss in sight." The article commences:
Flood damage around the great lakes this summer may get up to $1 billion or more.
There's a great, creeping flood under way. Water, rising steadily, is expected to be 5 feet and more above the 1934 level by summer. Big areas already are flooded or threatened.
What to do is a big question now worrying U.S. and Canadian governments.
Then the article goes on to give details which were not in the press dispatch from the Globe and Mail, and makes it pretty clear that the situation is extremely serious from the point of view of the United States, and I presume it is just as serious to Canadians. One paragraph says:
The threatened areas are finally getting Washington excited about it, too. Congressmen are needling the government for aid. The army corps of engineers is making surveys. The U.S. weather bureau is tightening up its storm-warning system on the lakes.
Then we find this significant sentence:
The state department last week got Canada to agree to a review of the problem.
The minister certainly should make a statement with regard to that, and let us know whether it is correct.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: Surely my hon. friend would not expect me to make a statement on a matter like that. I can deal with the problem generally, but that surely is a matter for the Secretary of State for External Affairs, particularly in view of the sentence he just has read.

Then the article goes on to deal with Canada's Long Lac and Ogoki power projects having diverted 5,000 cubic feet of water per second, and it also refers to Canada's Gut dam in the St. Lawrence river rapids just below lake Ontario which, it says, slows down the flow of Ontario's water to the sea, and thus adds several extra inches to the lakes' levels. Apparently the situation is extremely serious. I would ask the minister to make a statement to the house tonight in connection with this matter.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words in reply to the remarks the minister made at eight o'clock-in other

words, since it is now nearly half past ten I have been exercising the virtue of patience for over two hours-with reference to the need for augmenting the pensions of retired C.N.R. employees, particularly in the case of those who have only the basic $25 a month.
I spoke about this last Friday when the estimates of the minister were first called, and I endeavoured to make it clear at that time that there have been some improvements in the situation since we last discussed this matter in the house. I pointed out then, but it seems I must repeat it now, that although there are improvements for those still in the service, if they choose to avail themselves of those improvements, and although there are potential improvements for those already retired where their pensions were in part contributory, and therefore are more than $25 a month, it still remains that there is no improvement by virtue of the recent changes in the Canadian National pension rules for those already retired who have only the basic pension of $25 a month.
I respectfully suggest to the minister that to remind us of the improvements that have been made for others does not solve the problem or deal with the plight of the men who have only $25 a month. It is that group in particular whose case I continue to plead with the minister.
When he concluded the remarks he made at eight o'clock this evening the minister expressed the hope that what he had said would bring this discussion to an end, and that that would be the last word on it. I am sure he did not think that would be the case; I am sure he did not expect that I would cease pleading the case of men left in this most difficult position and drawing, as far as their railway pension is concerned, only $25 a month. My purpose in rising now is to express the hope that the minister will yet give further consideration to the situation of these retired employees.
The minister, as has been done on other occasions when this question has been raised, referred to the improvements in old age pension legislation that have taken place since we were discussing this same problem of the C.N.R. pensioners a year ago. Let me point out again that those improvements are available to other people as well, but in my view that does not relieve the Canadian National, which is owned by the government, of its obligation to these men, an obligation which arises in part from the fact that there has been such a tremendous increase in the cost of living since this $25 basic pension was first established.
The minister said tonight that under the new old age pension legislation it is possible
Supply-Transport
for those men who are getting only $25 a month from their C.N.R. pension to get a total of $65 a month by going on the old age pension as well. For simplicity's sake I presume he was speaking of single men, and I will do the same. I would point out to him that in the case of those between 65 and 69 they cannot get a total of $65 a month. There is a ceiling in the old age legislation which limits total income between ages 65 and 69 to $60 a month, so the $25 railway pension limits them to the amount they can draw under the Old Age Assistance Act. I would also point out thst some of these men do have small homes, or some other asset, that they have been able to build up across the years; and if that is the case that other asset, together with their $25 a month, in many cases denies them the opportunity of getting anything out of the old age assistance legislation whatever.
Then there is the case of those over 70, and there are quite a few of them. I ask the minister to note this situation which I think is most unfair. Let us take the case of two C.N.R. pensioners, one we will say, for example, drawing $100 a month C.N.R. pension and the other drawing just the $25 a month. They are both over 70. They both qualify for the old age security pension of $40 a month. In the case of the C.N.R. pensioner with the $100 a month who gets $40 old age security, it is still possible for him, with his $100 railway pension, to take advantage of the new rules and augment that $100 pension to a slightly higher amount. But the C.N.R. pensioner who is getting only $25 a month, when he gets his $40 old age security, cannot do anything to increase that $25 basic pension. It is there, and he cannot get it increased by any means under the new rules. So you have on the one hand a C.N.R. pensioner with $100 a month getting an extra $40, which puts him up to $140, and he may increase that amount a bit further. On the other hand you have the railway pensioner on $25 getting $40 old age security, which puts him up to $65; and he cannot get any more out of the C.N.R. pension fund, even under the changes that have come into effect at the present time. The unfairness to the $25 pensioner is surely obvious.
In passing I should point out that when we talk about retired employees with pensions of more than $25 a month being able to augment those pensions, it should be noted that this possibility depends upon whether they can make a certain contribution. Thus for many of these people it is a theoretical possibility which it may be hard for them to turn into a reality.
However, there is not even a theoretical possibility of any increase for those men who

Supply-Transport
are on the basic pension of only $25 a month. As I have already pointed out on several occasions, their number is something over 3,000 and I feel that the government still has a responsibility to those people.
In view of the statements the minister made tonight, I am not asking him to comment further at this time. I should prefer to hear from him in more favourable terms, and I hope he will give the matter further consideration. Surely he knew, when he expressed the hope that what he said tonight would be the end of this matter, that his hope would not be realized. Surely he would not, on second thought, ask any group of men on $25 a month to sit back and be satisfied with such a pension under today's conditions. And I know he does not expect those of us who have pleaded the case for these men to stop pleading it because of the kind of arguments that were put forth tonight.
The problem is still there; the plight of these men is there; the unfairness still exists; and I hope that even yet consideration will be given by the government to raising the $25 pension, particularly in the case of those already retired for whom there is no chance of improvement under the rules as they now stand.
Just one other word, and it is this: The minister suggested that this was a problem to be threshed out between the men and the Canadian National Railways. I agree that most aspects of employer-employee relations are best dealt with in that way. But it just so happens that, in the very nature of the case, once these men are retired and no longer working for the company, the normal negotiations that go on between employees, through their representatives, and the company, somehow or another do not seem to include the same attention for the plight of the retired men as is given to the needs of the men still in the service.
The minister must recognize that these men do need a voice pleading on their behalf and, what is more, that they need a ministerial ear to pay attention to that plea.
Mr. Chairman-

The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra dealt again with the question of the policy of the Canadian maritime commission with reference to the deep-sea fleet, and Canada's merchant navy. The policy of the commission has not changed-the hon. member seemed to be under the impression that it had- since the commission was established. It is true that the replacement plan has been altered, but that was because the shipping companies felt that it would be more profitable to build ships in Canada for St. Lawrence river and great lakes operation than to build fast cargo vessels for deep-sea operation. The cost of building deep-sea ships is far greater in Canada than in the United Kingdom and certain continental countries, and that is why it was found necessary to alter
That is for great lakes and St. Lawrence ships?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Yes. My hon. friend dealt with the question of the dual capacity of the deputy minister acting as chairman of the maritime commission and asked whether that was a firm policy of the government. That is not a firm policy of the government; the government has determined no policy in that regard. It so happened that at the time of the resignation of the former chairman conditions and circumstances were such that it was found advisable to operate the maritime commission under the arrangement which was then adopted. That action was supported by the fact that a large number of our ships had been transferred to United Kingdom registry, which meant much less work for the maritime commission than it would have had if the one hundred or more ships had remained under Canadian registry. That does not mean to say that should they come back under Canadian registry we will immediately change this policy, neither does it mean that the government is committed to continuing the deputy minister as chairman of the maritime commission.
My hon. friend wanted to know whether the Ming Sung ships were still under Canadian registry. As far as I know they are. If they were not there would be no way of protecting the mortgage.
There is not much way of protecting it now.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
That remains to be seen. My hon. friend wants a statement and he should let me make it. This is a matter which concerns external affairs, but I will give as much information as I have available. It would be a mistake to remove the Ming Sung ships from Canadian registry because we would then lose forever the mortgage which we hold against those ships. There may be some other method of saving the mortgage, but I do not know.
The hon. member asked whether the ships were still flying the Canadian flag. I am not able to answer that and I am sure nobody else is. I do not know where the ships are. I presume they are in Chinese communist waters, but I do not know what flag they are flying. Then my hon. friend wanted to know what steps are being taken to clear up this situation. That is easier said than done. Steps are being taken and careful consideration is being given, and has been given, by

Gold Mining
the government to the whole matter. I am not able to go beyond that because other ministers are dealing with the question.
I can assure my hon. friend that the Canada Shipping Act has been carefully studied. The Department of Justice has been taking an active part, as has the Department of Finance and the Department of External Affairs. The government would like to be able to say that the matter is being cleared up, but there are international difficulties that do not make it so easy.
The matter of high water levels on the great lakes and the upper St. Lawrence river pertains to another department. This department is concerned in so far as the Gut dam is involved. It is a serious problem, and is created by precipitation and the diversion of waters into the great lakes, and to some extent by the Gut dam. All the artificial causes added together are but a drop in the bucket compared to the precipitation or other natural causes. If the Gut dam were removed the effect would be to raise the level about five and one-half inches; but if that were done, particularly at this time, it might cause serious trouble downstream, particularly if the Ottawa river rose as it did last year and some years ago. Serious flood conditions might occur in the downstream areas.
This is unquestionably an international matter, and it is being considered by the two countries. Were the minister of external affairs here he could say how far the talks between Canada and the United States have gone. There is provision under the great lakes-St. Lawrence seaway proposal to guard against this kind of situation by means of regulatory methods provided for in the plans and specifications.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: With respect to clause 2, I note that it extends the application of the act for two more years, but in addition to that it seems to make certain changes so that the basis of computation will be different than it was previously. speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext:
The purpose of this amendment is to extend the application of the act to the years 1952 and 1953 and to clarify the conditions under which a mine operator may elect as a base year the calendar years 1948, 1949 or 1950. The intent of the present act was that the year chosen as the base year should be one in which the mine had been in operation for a full calendar year and had during that time been in production for more than six months. As the act at present reads, a mine whose first year of production commenced subsequent to January 1 and prior to June 30 of any of the above years may choose that year as its base year, thus gaining an advantage that was never intended.
There are five mines in this category and each elected as its base year the first year of operation which in every instance was less than twelve months. This amendment will mean a decrease in assistance payable of $69,456. The mines affected are Howe Sound Exploration Company Limited, Quesabe Mines Limited, Giant Yellowknife

Gold Mines Limited, Campbell Red Lake Mines Limited, and Consolidated Duquesne Mining Company Limited. The last mentioned is not affected financially. Giant Yellowknife Gold Mines Limited will gain $2,960 and the others will lose substantial amounts.
